newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus shipping safety focussed in EU talks.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus shipping safety focussed in EU talks.

text.p: Cyprus has started to recruit international surveyors to check safety standards of Cyprus-flagged ships in 50 ports as part of a drive to meet an international convention imposing minimum standards.
A Cypriot government official said on Thursday the island hoped that by early next year it would be able to fully check the safety standards of the large fleet.

"It is no secret that the Cypriot shipping register is still not in a position to fully check the standards of safety of all its fleet," said Cypriot Communications and Works Minister Adamos Adamides.

Adamides, speaking at a news conference with Irish Defence and Marine Minister Sean Barrett and Neil Kinnock, a member of the European Commission responsible for transport, said a network of international surveyors is currently being recruited.
"We expect full implementation of this scheme to be completed in the middle of next year," he said.
The eastern Mediterranean island boasts a shipping registry of 27 million gross tonnes, making it the fourth largest in the world.

In the past its image was tarnished by lax registration requirements and a failure to adopt international safety standards. Last year the government ratified an international convention imposing minimum safety standards on all vessels.
Kinnock and Barrett were in Cyprus as part of the "structured dialogue" the island has started with the E.U., with which it hopes to start accession talks with in early 1998.
The structured dialogue is supposed to prepare a candidate state for a smoother accession course.
A main stumbling block between the two parties is expected to be the status of offshore companies on the island -- many of them shipping firms that contribute substantial income to the local economy.
Kinnock said the two sides needed to reach a "strong understanding" on the issue.
Cyprus offers a flat tax rate of 4.25 percent on net income for offshore companies setting up on the island and offers exemptions from value added tax, which is eight percent.
By contrast, local companies pay 20 percent corporate tax on net income up to 40,000 pounds ($85,600) and 25 percent above that figure.
"Cyprus is a major shipping power," said Kinnock. "We have rules in the community to try to ensure fair competition in all commercial activities.

"It is going to be necessary for us to develop a strong understanding and preparatory development in order to ensure that there is no possiblity of the Cyprus admission to the EU having unfortunate or negative consequences in terms of fair competition," he said.

Adamides told Reuters that Cyprus will define its position on the issue next year. "We are fully in agreement as regards the safety standards. But we do believe that non-distortive measures should be taken for this fleet to remain in Cyprus provided that safety standards are kept," he said. ($=0.465 pounds)
